name: African socialism
summary: African socialism is the family of socialist doctrines adopted by African leaders around independence in the 1950s-70s. Its shared claim is that precolonial African communities were communal and largely classless, so socialism is an indigenous African inheritance and a third way between Western capitalism and Soviet communism, with class struggle rejected as a European idea. Nyerere's Ujamaa, Senghor's socialist humanism, Touré's and Nkrumah's more Marxist versions and Kenya's Sessional Paper No. 10 differ on markets, planning, the party and alignment.
scope: The doctrines the defining sources (Britannica, the East African Academy's 1970 summary and bibliography, and Draisma's study of it and education) call African socialism: post-independence socialisms of the 1950s-70s that root socialism in African communal tradition and reject class struggle. They name three strands (Andrain, via the 1970 summary): African Marxism (Touré, Nkrumah), socialist humanism (Senghor, Dia) and the social-welfare state (Obote, Azikiwe, Nyerere, Kenya's Sessional Paper No. 10). The profile follows the texts the sources make canonical and that are read in full here: Nyerere's Ujamaa essay and the Arusha Declaration (1967), and Kenya's Sessional Paper No. 10 (1965). Senghor's and Nkrumah's own books are known only through the sources describing them. Excluded: later Marxist-Leninist African regimes, critics' accounts such as Babu's, and the separate catalog ideologies Ujamaa, Nkrumaism, Negritude and Pan-Africanism, whose own sources do not speak for this one.

missingStatements.text: Traditional village communities, not imported ideology, are the proper foundation for a modern socialist society.
missingStatements.rationale: Nyerere's essay bases African socialism on the extended family and traditional community, and the central claim of the ideology is that socialism is indigenous.

missingStatements.text: Land should belong to the community or nation, with people holding it only so long as they use it.
missingStatements.rationale: Nyerere holds that traditional land rights lasted only with use, and says freehold ownership is a foreign concept leading to speculation.

missingStatements.text: Political leaders should be barred from holding company shares, extra salaries or rental property.
missingStatements.rationale: The Arusha leadership code states exactly these bars so leaders do not live off another person's work.

notes: Searched the Arusha Declaration, Nyerere's essays (Ujamaa), Kenya's Sessional Paper No. 10 (1965), Britannica and two scholarly summaries for ownership, markets, planning, land, work, class, democracy, one-party rule, religion, race, aid, non-alignment, taxes, welfare, unions and rural villages. Senghor's and Nkrumah's books were only lending copies and were not read; Padmore's 1931 booklet was set aside as a communist-phase work he later repudiated. Earlier answers resting on inference were nulled; adherents split on public ownership, collective farming and one-party rule.
